concepts.title: Motivation for Learning-Based Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based methods address the failures of traditional motion models by implicitly exploiting semantic properties and complex image cues.
concepts.content: While model-based methods for motion estimation are derived from first principles, they often rely on assumptions that do not hold in real-world scenarios. Modeling errors can occur due to the failure of the brightness constancy assumption, the presence of occlusions, shadows, illumination changes, and deformable surfaces. Additionally, traditional computations often use approximations like finite size discrete convolutions. Learning-based models can implicitly exploit motion-relevant cues that are difficult to model explicitly, such as monocular depth cues and semantic priors (e.g., buildings are stationary, while people are deformable).
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional mathematical models often fail in complex environments with shadows, occlusions, or non-rigid motion. Learning-based approaches allow systems to discover patterns and semantic rules that first-principles equations cannot easily capture.
concepts.recap_md: - Overcomes limitations of the brightness constancy assumption and modeling approximations.

key_passage.text: The reason is that the models make a number of assumptions that are not always true. Also, there are other sources of information that can reveal properties about motion that cannot be modeled but that can be learned.

motivation.text: Causes of modeling errors include failure of the brightness constancy assumption; the presence of occlusions, shadows and changes in illumination; new structures appearing due to changes in the resolution as a result of motion, deformable surfaces; and so on. Those semantic properties can be implicitly exploited by a learning-based model.

concepts.title: Overview of Learning-Based Approaches
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based motion estimation is divided into supervised models using training data and unsupervised models that learn without ground truth.
concepts.content: Learning-based approaches for motion estimation build upon established computer vision concepts and are generally categorized into two families: supervised models and unsupervised models. Supervised models learn to estimate motion by utilizing a database of training examples with known ground truth. In contrast, unsupervised models learn to estimate motion without the need for labeled training data.
concepts.motivation_md: Categorizing learning methods helps distinguish between those that require expensive, labeled ground-truth data and those that can learn directly from raw video sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - Supervised models require training databases with ground truth motion.

key_passage.text: Learning-based approaches rely on many of the concepts we introduced in the previous chapters. We will differentiate between two big families of models: supervised models that learn to estimate motion using a database of training examples, and unsupervised models that learn to estimate motion without training data.

concepts.title: Supervised Models for Optical Flow Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Supervised optical flow estimation uses datasets with ground truth motion to train models to predict motion directly from input frames.
concepts.content: The simplest formulation for learning optical flow involves using a dataset of image sequences associated with ground truth optical flow. These datasets are constructed using synthetic data, lidar sensors, or human annotations. While ground truth data was previously used primarily for evaluation, supervised models use it to train the system to predict motion directly from the input frames.
concepts.motivation_md: By providing a model with the 'correct' answer (ground truth), it can learn the complex mapping between pixel intensity changes and actual physical motion through backpropagation.
concepts.recap_md: - Utilizes synthetic, lidar-based, or human-annotated datasets for training.

key_passage.text: The simplest formulation for learning to estimate optical flow is when we have available a dataset of image sequences with associated ground truth optical flow.

concepts.title: FlowNet Architecture
concepts.one_liner: FlowNet is an end-to-end neural network architecture that estimates optical flow directly from a pair of image frames.
concepts.content: FlowNet is one of the first neural network approaches to estimate optical flow from two frames using the function: $$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$$ (see figure: In FlowNet the direct approach estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames.) The architecture is simple and makes no specific assumptions about architectural priors. It is trained end-to-end using ground truth optical flow to learn the estimation process directly from the input image pair.
concepts.motivation_md: FlowNet demonstrated that a standard convolutional neural network could learn to solve the optical flow problem end-to-end without needing hand-engineered features or traditional optimization steps.
concepts.recap_md: - Estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames using a simple end-to-end architecture.

key_passage.text: One of the first approaches to use this formulation with neural networks was FlowNet. The direct approach learns to estimate optical flow directly from a pair of frames. This architecture makes no assumptions about which architectural priors are needed to compute optical flow from images.

concepts.title: Modular Optical Flow Architectures
concepts.one_liner: Modular architectures for optical flow integrate traditional steps like feature extraction and cost volumes into end-to-end trainable networks.
concepts.content:
A common approach in supervised motion estimation is to define an architecture that mirrors traditional procedural steps: 
- Extract features from each image using a pair of networks with shared weights, often via a feature pyramid. 
- Form a 3D cost volume indicating local visual evidence of a match between the two images for each possible pixel position. 
- Apply a CNN to aggregate costs over the volume to estimate the best optical flow for each pixel. 
- Use a coarse-to-fine estimation procedure where coarse-scale flow warps features at a finer scale for refined cost volume computation. 
(see figure: Motion estimation. (1) Extract features from each image; (2) compute a 3D cost volume; and (3) aggregate the cost volume in order to estimate the best optical flow for each pixel.) 
Unlike traditional matching or gradient-based methods, these modular architectures are trained end-to-end to minimize optical flow error relative to ground truth.
concepts.motivation_md: By combining the structural insights of traditional computer vision (like cost volumes and pyramids) with the learning power of CNNs, these architectures often achieve higher accuracy and better generalization than simple direct models.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines feature pyramids, 3D cost volumes, and coarse-to-fine refinement.

key_passage.text: Another common approach is to define an architecture that follows the same steps as traditional approaches: Extract features from each image using a pair of networks with shared weights. Form a 3D cost volume indicating the local visual evidence of a match between the two images for each possible pixel position. Train and apply a CNN to aggregate (process) the costs over the cost volume in order to estimate a single best optical flow for each pixel position.

motivation.text: Other variations over this architecture incorporate some of the concepts we studied before, such as coarse-to-fine refinement, matching, and smoothing. The main difference between the matching-based and gradient-based methods described earlier is that instead of using predefined functions, the architectures are trained end-to-end to minimize the optical flow error when compared with ground truth data.

concepts.title: Endpoint Error
concepts.one_liner: The endpoint error is the average distance between estimated optical flow vectors and ground-truth vectors across an image.
concepts.content: In supervised optical flow estimation, the most common loss function is the endpoint error. This is defined as the average distance, over the whole image, between the estimated optical flow vector $(\hat{u},\hat{v})$ and the ground-truth vector $(u,v)$: $$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \right) = \sum_{n,m} (\hat{u}[n,m] - u[n,m])^2 + (\hat{v}[n,m] - v[n,m])^2$$ The sum is calculated over all pixels in the image, where each pixel has an associated estimated optical flow $(\hat{u}[n,m],\hat{v}[n,m])$. [FIGURE:94e55f574651d9ae | ]
concepts.motivation_md: To train a neural network for motion, we need a mathematical way to penalize the difference between the predicted motion and the actual motion. Endpoint error provides a simple Euclidean distance metric for this purpose.
concepts.recap_md: - Standard loss function for supervised optical flow training.

concepts.title: Handling Occlusions in Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Estimating an occlusion map alongside optical flow helps account for pixels that are hidden or revealed as objects move.
concepts.content: One of the challenges for estimating optical flow is that, as objects move, they will occlude some pixels from the background and reveal new ones. Therefore, together with the estimated flow it is also convenient to detect occluded pixels. If we have ground truth data, we can train a function to estimate optical flow and the occlusion map from two frames: $$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \hat{\mathbf{o}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$$
concepts.motivation_md: In dynamic scenes, moving objects frequently cover or uncover parts of the background. Standard optical flow assumes every pixel in the first frame has a corresponding pixel in the second; identifying occlusions allows the model to handle areas where this assumption fails.
concepts.recap_md: - Moving objects create occlusions and disocclusions that complicate pixel-wise correspondence.

concepts.title: Datasets for Optical Flow Training
concepts.one_liner: Supervised motion estimation relies on synthetic and specialized real-world datasets to provide the difficult-to-collect ground truth for optical flow.
concepts.content: The biggest challenge of using a supervised model for motion estimation is that ground truth data is very hard to collect. The largest existing datasets are synthetic 3D scenes with moving objects that can be rendered, which provide perfect ground truth data to train the regression function. Examples include the Middlebury dataset, which contains six real and synthetic sequences where real flow was obtained by tracking hidden fluorescent texture. The KITTI dataset contains real motion recorded from a moving car. The MPI Sintel contains synthetic sequences designed to look realistic. Finally, the Flying Chairs dataset is a synthetic dataset consisting of random chairs pasted over background images with affine transformations applied. Because these sequences are easy to generate, they allow for a very large number of training sequences, enabling competitive performance when training neural networks.
concepts.motivation_md: Ground truth optical flow cannot be easily recorded in the real world. Researchers use synthetic environments and specialized tracking techniques to create the large-scale data necessary for training supervised deep learning models.
concepts.recap_md: - Ground truth for optical flow is difficult to obtain, leading to a reliance on synthetic data.

concepts.title: Unsupervised Learning of Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised learning estimates optical flow by assuming brightness constancy, spatial smoothness, and geometric constraints from camera motion.
concepts.content: Collecting ground truth data is the Achilles heel for learning-based approaches, particularly for optical flow which cannot be recorded directly. Real data collection is expensive and nonscalable. Unsupervised methods for training an optical flow model instead make assumptions about dynamic image formation: (1) when motion is due only to camera motion, the optical flow must fit the equations of projected motion; (2) the appearances of objects and surfaces do not change due to motion (brightness constancy assumption); and (3) the optical flow is expected to be smooth over regions, with sharp variations occurring only along occlusion boundaries.
concepts.motivation_md: Because obtaining ground truth optical flow for real-world scenes is often impossible or prohibitively expensive, unsupervised methods allow models to learn motion patterns directly from raw video by enforcing physical and geometric consistency.
concepts.recap_md: - Unsupervised flow estimation avoids the need for ground truth by using physical assumptions.

key_passage.text: Unsupervised methods for training an optical flow model will make some assumptions about dynamic image formation. Those assumptions will be similar to the ones we have presented all along this chapter- (1) when the motion is due only to camera motion, the optical flow will have to fit the equations of the projected motion that provide constraints that can be used to train a model; (2) we can assume that the appearances of objects and surfaces in the scene do not change due to motion (brightness constancy assumption); and (3) we can expect the optical flow to be smooth over regions, although with sharp variations along occlusion boundaries.

concepts.title: Photometric Loss
concepts.one_liner: Photometric loss measures the reconstruction error between a target frame and a source frame warped by the predicted displacement.
concepts.content: One typical formulation consists in learning to predict the displacement from frame 1 to frame 2, so that if we warp frame 1 we minimize the reconstruction error of frame 2. This is achieved by using the photometric loss: $$L_{photo}(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_2 (x+\hat{u},y+\hat{v}) - \ell_1 (x,y)) \right| ^2$$ where $\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$.
concepts.motivation_md: In the absence of ground truth labels, photometric loss provides a self-supervised signal by checking if the predicted motion can successfully 'undo' the movement between two frames.
concepts.recap_md: - Photometric loss quantifies how well the predicted flow aligns two consecutive video frames.

concepts.title: Learning with Photometric Loss
concepts.one_liner: Learning involves minimizing photometric loss over large video collections, potentially incorporating robust norms or occlusion weights.
concepts.content: The learning is done by searching over the parameter space for the parameters $\theta$ that minimize the photometric loss over a large collection of videos. The photometric loss can also be replaced by the L1 or other robust norms. If the network also predicts occlusions, the photometric loss can include a weight that cancels the contribution of occluded pixels to the loss. The network can also take as input multiple frames and not just two.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard photometric loss can be sensitive to outliers and occlusions. Refining the loss function with robust norms or occlusion masks makes the training process more stable and accurate in complex scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Parameters are optimized to minimize reconstruction error across video datasets.
